#98713. Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (655 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto 📈 Bullish 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine.
  • Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
  • We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company announced plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company announced plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a company with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

Sources indicate that the UC3 originally introduced in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t declared any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

According to recent reports, in much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

It has been revealed that I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

Sources indicate that I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost issue - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A GREAT UNDERSHIRT is my first line of defense against sweat, stains, and overheating. It’s like the menswear equivalent of SPF. I learned that the hard way years ago, when I wore a flimsy cotton tee under a light-blue dress shirt to a summer wedding and, by cocktail hour, looked like I’d run a 10K instead of walked down the aisle. Never again. Now, if I’m layering under a dress shirt or sweater, I want something that works hard without me ever thinking about it. The best undershirts are so comfortable, I forget they’re even on. Unlike cheap, bulky options that ride up, trap heat, or lose their shape after a few washes, the real standouts are lightweight, moisture-wicking, and cut with a trim fit that stays put without squeezing the life out of you. They also tuck away neatly into trousers and save your other shirts from pit stains.

Recent findings suggest that to find the GOATs, our fashion team and I tested more than 50 styles—everything from V-neck tees and tank tops to classic white crewnecks—wearing them under button-downs, sweaters, and even on their own. The winners disappear under your clothes like a good stunt double, regulate temperature like built-in AC, and keep you looking cool, calm, and collected from your morning commute to last call.

Industry observers note that hanes is perhaps the most famous undershirt brand on the planet. I’ve been wearing its undergarments since I was about 10 years old, and over the time, they've just become better in terms of fit and feel. For example, I’ve been wearing Hanes’ performance undershirt for four months, and it’s consistently comfortable, breathable, and snug in all the right places.

In a recent development, the shoulders sit perfectly without pulling, the chest drapes close without clinging, and the sleeves are tailored to follow your arms without cutting into your biceps. When an undershirt feels this light, I brace myself for it to be flimsy and tear like tissue, but it's impressively solid—and I didn’t even sweat in it. Unlike other undershirts that I’ve tested, this one has a structured collar and hem that keeps its shape. The polyester-rayon fabric is extra smooth and cool to the touch, even after wearing it for hours at the office. I also appreciate that the fabric blend is much lighter in weight than a traditional cotton undershirt.

According to recent reports, after putting it through at least eight washes, I noticed that the fabric didn’t fade or shrink. One way I preserve it is by letting it air dry instead of tossing it in the dryer under high heat. It’s long enough to tuck in and doesn’t bunch under an overshirt. Since it's blended with a hint of stretch, I could grab a box off a high shelf without any restriction. Hanes uses the same double-needle stitching to reinforce the neck, sleeves, and hem as with their regular undershirts. This will stand up to years of washing and wearing with steady use. It only comes in white, but you can wear it with so many different fits—solo or layered.

Read More: Best T-Shirts for Men.

According to recent reports, mack Weldon was founded to reinvent men's underwear and loungewear with better fabric blends and quality construction. Take its V-neck style undershirt that I've been wearing for a couple months now. It’s cut from a polyamide-elastane blend—the same kind of technical fabric in our favorite workout clothes. It’s got that silky-soft hand feel with real stretch baked in. I can lift my arms, reach overhead, and wrestle into a jacket on the subway, and I don’t feel any tugging in the arms. The neckline sits low enough to disappear when I don’t want it to be seen under my dress shirts, but not so deep it feels flimsy or overly delicate.

In a recent development, what really sold me, though, is the breathability. Even under my chunky sweaters with some heft, I never break a sweat or find myself needing to flap my knit like I'm trying to cool off. Since it has a slim fit, it sits close to my skin without being tight, but stays dry when I’m making my way through the muggy subway or sitting in non-air-conditioned areas at the office. I tossed it in the wash at least six times and the white still looks just as good as the day it came out the pack.

It has been revealed that tommy John V-neck undershirt is step above your average option when it comes to polished layering. Its slim cut and modal fabric give it shape and structure, so it skims the body without feeling tight—perfect for showing off a chest workout without clinging in an unflattering way.

According to recent reports, one of the best features is how it tucks. The snug-but-not-tight fit keeps the shirt neatly in place under dress shirts or sweaters, so you don’t get bunching or riding up. This makes it ideal for formal and office-ready attire, where a clean, smooth base layer is essential. It’s also stretchy without being too thin and has yet to pill, five washes later. I recommend letting it air dry, so it doesn’t shrink or become tight since the undershirt has a slim fit.

Industry observers note that after multiple wears, the V collar doesn’t give “bacon neck”, which makes it look worn-out. It sits closer to the neck than Mack Weldon’s version, but I still can hide it by closing the top two buttons of my dress shirt. I love the buttery-soft feel, which is breathable and light even in warmer 70-degree temps.

A major qualm with undershirts is their neckline can easily get ratted through the wash. We found Jockey's Made in America tees to keep a strong neckline and provide overall durability as an everyday undershirt. This is one of those cases where it's worth paying the extra bucks for an American-made garment.

It has been revealed that the Made in America factor isn't just for show. The quality that comes with it is apparent. The construction is clean and the fabric is thick enough that this undershirt can double as a plain white tee. So if you ever need to shed a layer or two, you can fall back on this as a base layer t-shirt. You can even style it on a hot day with just a pair of shorts.

Recent findings suggest that more importantly, we found that Jockey has nailed the standard 100% cotton plain white undershirt in the best way possible. It feels like a traditional soft cotton tee, but after putting it through the wash and dry cycles more than a dozen times, it managed to withstand all the wear and tear and stay intact, proving its durability. The fabric even has a tech built-in to reduce piling and fading. And I love that the cotton is engineered to be able to wick away sweat in a heartbeat to keep me fresh all day. The only thing is that the fabric isn't wrinkle-resistant, so store these shirts carefully.

In a recent development, ATEK’s Stay Cooling undershirt is engineered for guys who run hot. The nylon-spandex blend feels slick and technical—almost like performance base-layer gear—but that’s exactly why it works. It wicks sweat fast, dries quickly, and stays smooth under slimmer dress shirts without bunching or clinging. I’ve been wearing it while commuting and traveling since 2021, especially on days when I’m bouncing between the subway, the office, and post-work aims. The stretch makes it easy to move in, and after dozens of washes, it hasn’t shrunk or warped.

Industry observers note that gollayan put it through even tougher paces. He wore it under tailored dress shirts during long shoot days and under knit polos in the summer heat, noting that it kept sweat marks at bay and didn’t show through lightweight fabrics. He also flagged how well it holds its shape through the torso—no bacon-neck collar, no sagging by 4 p.m. If you love the soft, matte hand-feel of classic cotton, this one may feel a bit slick and synthetic. But that’s the trade-off for serious cooling power.

Sources indicate that there has never been another brand with more hype around it than the early 1990s "My Calvins" undergarment campaign. But Calvin Klein's classic ribbed tank is not just hype, it is actually a really solid undershirt. If you prefer the minimal fabric feel of a tank or you just wear them when it's hot out then Calvins are hard to beat. And these, as undershirts, are practically perfect in terms of fabric, fit, and durability.

According to recent reports, the full cotton fabric is stretchy despite having no built-in elastane or spandex. We love its soft-to-touch quality as well as natural breathability, the latter helps with wicking away sweat. The classic fit we found is slim without being constricting and they're just long enough to be tucked in if you need to but they can hang out without showing. The classic scoop neckline and seaming have also lasted well, and the fabric, even after over a dozen wash and dry cycles, has remained as stretchy, soft, and breezy.

For layering, we love putting it underneath a button-down or sweater/sweatshirt, though if you’re prone to underarm, we’d advise against this undershirt as your go-to.

Recent findings suggest that bugatchi’s crew neck tee is another great option that blurs the line between undershirt and standalone tee, but it leans more dressy than most. Made from a silky-soft Pima cotton, it has a luxe feel and fluid drape that’s more cocktail hour than couch rotting. I’ve worn it tucked into slacks with dress shoes for a fancy dinner, and it held its own. The fabric skims the body without clinging, and the finish reads sleek, not sporty.

It doesn’t have a durable ribbed collar like other dressier T-shirts, but it has a clean binding, which keeps its shape and frames the neck well. Compared to Reigning Champ’s athletic cut, this tee offers a touch more room in the torso, which flatters buffer guys. It layers neatly under jackets, but isn’t skin-tight. Out of all the undershirts on this list, this one has the best color options. When I'm heading into the city for dinner, I go with the mint to pair with cream dress pants for a clean, sharp ensemble. But for weekend errands or a coffee run, I throw on the air blue with jeans.

It has been revealed that gap has long been my go-to for affordable basics that punch above their price point. This undershirt is no different. While it’s not the trendiest or most technical, the shirt is made with an ultra-light, superfine jersey that’s buttery smooth, breathable, and almost weightless. It feels so nice and comfy that I lounge and sleep in it too. Unlike your average undershirt, which can feel a little thick or rough over time, this one stays silky and cool after multiple wears, making it perfect for layering under a blazer or shacket. Or, you could just throw it on to kick back on the couch.

The straight fit is a major win for guys who want an undershirt that feels natural rather than overly snug or restrictive. The looser cut drapes smoothly over the body without awkward bunching, so you can wear it all day. In terms of the quality after washing, I have never seen the fabric pill. This kind of cotton manages to stay incredibly soft, cycle after cycle, speaking to its high quality.

Sources indicate that at first glance, Reigning Champ’s jersey slim T-shirt might look like your everyday summer tee, but don’t be fooled. Yes, it has that easy, breezy fabric you want in a lightweight layer, but it’s not filmy, too thin, or see-through. It’s made from premium cotton that’s both smooth and breathable, yet structured enough that it retains its shape. I've tossed it in the wash at least four times now, and it still comes out looking good as upcoming. The cut is slim and subtly tapered at the hem, which looks sharp on athletic builds and lean frames.

In a recent development, unlike looser, floppier collars that stretch out after a few cycles, this one is topped with a rib-bound collar that stays in place. It’s one of the only lightweight undershirts we tested where the collar didn’t droop, curl, or widen after wash two. I’ve worn it solo with shorts and jeans for coffee runs and quick errands. It also handled light activity in the park without showing any sweat and still looked fresh after hours of wear. Bonus: The color selection offers a number of neutrals that work for every outfit.

If you’re looking for the most breathable undershirt, it’s hard to beat the Uniqlo AIRism T-shirt. It’s made from a lightweight, high-tech fabric that consists of a polyester-elastane blend that dries quickly and helps regulate body temperature to keep you cool and comfy all day. I wore the tee during a full-day shoot under a denim overshirt and didn’t overheat once even under direct sun and studio lights.

Industry observers note that it wicked away sweat faster than I expected and, more impressively, dried completely by the time I was back indoors. I also put it through a few airport and train travel days and the stretch fit held its shape, didn’t smell funky, and kept me feeling way fresher than any basic cotton tee could. Whether you’re layering it under a button-down or wearing it solo on a hot commute, it keeps you cool, not clammy, even in peak humidity.

In a recent development, the ribbed texture is what really sets this tee apart from your average undershirt. It adds natural stretch and recovery, which means the shirt contours to your body, especially around the chest, arms and torso, without feeling tight or restrictive. The result? A more sculpted, flattering fit that holds its shape throughout the day. I tested it on a few hours-long photoshoots and can confirm: it doesn’t ride up, it breathes well, and the collar doesn’t sag by mid-afternoon.

It has been revealed that the fabric itself, a soft organic and recycled cotton-blend jersey, has just the right amount of weight. The fine ribbing, which creates raised vertical lines that look like subtle ridges, adds structure without veering into ’90s tank top territory, and the slim fit gives it that clean, tailored base layer vibe. It’s also a subtle style flex: If you shed your overshirt, this undershirt doesn’t look like a throwaway white tee. It actually holds its own, especially when paired with jeans or trousers.

If you’re looking for a classic cotton undershirt that feels premium but not flashy, Brooks Brothers’ Supima Cotton V-Neck is it. It’s not built for performance like Mack Weldon’s tech-forward v-neck; it leans hard into comfort and breathability. Produced from Supima cotton, it’s noticeably smoother, softer, and more durable than other cotton shirts. It doesn’t hug the body as tightly, which actually makes it more forgiving on paunchier guts and more comfortable for long days on the move. This is the undershirt for guys who want something that disappears under button-ups; more work meeting than gym locker room.

I tested it under a white oxford shirt for a photoshoot at the office. The v-neck stayed completely hidden, even with the top two buttons undone, and the fit was trim enough that it didn’t bunch or add bulk under the shirt. Even under hot studio lights, I didn’t feel like I was sweating bullets. After three washes at home (cold wash, low tumble dry), the softness held up. It stayed smooth against the skin, with no pilling, collar warping or shrinkage. The seams stayed flat and clean, and the fabric has just enough weight to feel substantial, but still light enough to hide under thinner shirting.

Of all the undershirts we’ve tested, Fruit of the Loom’s 8-Pack easily provides the most value per wear. While it’s not as soft or moisture-wicking as more expensive shirts we’ve tried, it has a polyester-cotton blend that’s still comfortable and breathable enough to get you through the day. It doesn’t feel plastic-y, like other budget shirts we’ve tried. Rather, they have a natural cotton feel. Plus, the polyester blend does a competent job of wicking away sweat and helps keep its shape.

It has been revealed that the Skims Classic T-shirt is a jack of all trades because it works as a base layer, a solo tee, or even a sleep shirt—it’s that comfortable. It offers stretch, meaning it moves with you, whether you’re lounging at home, running errands, or layering it under a jacket. This kind of flexibility makes it far more versatile than a standard undershirt, which can sometimes feel stiff or lose its shape over time.

The fabric is also lightweight and super breathable, so you won’t sweat if you decide to catch some Z’s in it. Unlike oversized loungewear tees or super tight compression shirts, this one sits in the middle ground with its classic fit and crew neck. It’s tailored enough to look clean under a cardigan but still relaxed to wear with joggers or jeans for an easy off-duty look.

Recent findings suggest that the key to the 72-Hour Tee is its merino wool fabric. Huckberry engineered this tee to utilize the natural features of merino wool, which is breathable, moisture-wicking, odor-resistant, and temperature-regulating. The goal of the 72-Hour Tee was to create an undershirt that you can wear for three days straight without getting gross. Our testers wore it during long flights as long as 16 hours overseas. While we initially didn’t like the neckline or the hem—we did find that the 72-Hour Tee managed to stay hidden in our outer garments. And with its merino build, the fabric passed our tests of smell, sweat, cooling, and softness even after hours of non-stop wear. We also found that the fabric is soft and doesn’t itch, and could withstand wash cycles like a pro.

Sources indicate that sometimes you need an extra thick base layer to build your outfit on top of. Enter the Field-Spec Cotton Heavy Tee from Buck Mason. It's made from a 100% cotton jersey fabric that was inspired by old rugby jerseys, which is twice as thick as the fabric of regular T-shirts.

It's the perfect undershirt for cold days or a plain T-shirt for rugged pursuits. It's cut in a classic fit that is slightly boxy but the sleeves are not too long. This is a heartier undershirt for those times when a light cotton or blend won't do, but you don't want to wear it for athletic activities or in extreme cold. That thick cotton will just absorb all your sweat and weigh you down if you're working out and put you at risk in the extreme cold.

Industry observers note that the classic choice. Soft, breathable, and great for everyday wear. Look for Pima or Supima cotton—they’ve got longer fibers which means they’re softer, smoother, and way more durable than your run-of-the-mill cotton. The longer the fiber, the less fraying and pilling, so your tee stays looking fresh for way longer. That mentioned, if you’re going 100% cotton, just know that while it’s still super breathable, it won’t dry as fast as those high-tech synthetic fabrics.

Sources indicate that if you're an active guy, your undershirt material should also have a level of stretch (typically 5% or less)—courtesy of elastane or spandex—to help with flexibility and maintaining shape. If it is good quality cotton that you need then just plain old supple cotton will do the trick—it even gets cozier with age. If you like a tighter fit though, you should look for a blend with stretch in it.

According to recent reports, super soft, moisture-wicking, and great for layering. Modal and Tencel feel much silkier and cooler against the skin than the other materials we’ve tested, making them ideal for dress shirts or warm climates.

It has been revealed that surprisingly breathable and temperature-regulating. It’s great to wear year-round and compared to other fabrics on this list, it does a better job at keeping you smelling fresh, especially when breaking a sweat.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to drying and moisture-wicking, performance blends (like polyester, nylon, and elastane mixes) are the best in class compared to other fabrics on this list. That’s because they are engineered to pull sweat away from your skin and evaporate quickly. So if you need something for intense workouts or humid conditions, synthetic blends will keep you the driest.

Recent findings suggest that undershirts come in three main styles—crewneck, V-neck, and tank tops (A-shirts)—each designed for different layering needs, body types, and personal preferences. Choosing the right one can affect everything from comfort and breathability to how well your outer layers look.

In a recent development, the classic undershirt style features a round neckline that sits at the base of the neck. This is best for guys who want to fully cover their chest, while blending under crewneck sweaters, sweatshirts, and casual shirts. This also prevents chest hair from showing through thin shirts.

An undershirt with a V-shaped neckline, designed to stay hidden under an unbuttoned shirt or deeper-cut sweaters. It’s perfect for those who want a low-profile look and prefer to leave the top button of their dress shirt undone, so it’s almost invisible unlike crewnecks. V-Neck undershirts allow more breathability at the neck, especially in warmer weather.

In a recent development, on the other hand, we have tank tops—a sleeveless undershirt with wide shoulder straps and a scooped neckline. This style is often cut the lowest, to the chest, and highlights the least under another cloth or on its own. It’s perfect for guys who want less bulk, more arm mobility and extra breathability in hot weather.

Undershirts come in a range of fits, each with different benefits depending on personal preference and outfit choice.

Recent findings suggest that this fit is close to the body, but not skin-tight. It’s a go-to option if you like a clean, tailored look, making it ideal for layering under dress shirts since it won’t bunch up.

In a recent development, this fit is tighter than slim fit but still comfortable. It works well under fitted clothing but doesn’t feel restrictive. Cotton-blend undershirts with a little stretch (spandex or elastane) excel here.

It has been revealed that looser and more breathable, offering more movement than slim or snug fits. Works well for casual outfits but can bunch up under fitted dress shirts.

According to recent reports, the least restrictive, but can feel bulky under layers. On the flip side, it's great for lounging or wearing on its own.

Industry observers note that since 2021, I’ve worked alongside our fashion team—led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan—to test more than 50 undershirts at the office, beneath sweaters on chilly nights, layered under jackets, or even rocking them solo in the spring-summer months. We graded each undershirt on style, comfort, price, versatility, and overall performance. That meant paying close attention to moisture-wicking ability, stretch and recovery, breathability, and durability. To make sure our picks worked beyond our own closets, we also gathered feedback from testers across different body types and fit preferences. We also conferred with menswear expert Ted Stafford, who's spent decades evaluating everything from tailoring to boots. His expertise, along with our in-the-field testing, helped us lock in the 16 best undershirts for men that actually live up to the hype.

Recent findings suggest that while most undershirts for men are designed to be thin and worn as a base layer beneath other garments, they can also be worn alone as just a T-shirt or a tank top in certain situations. For instance, a high-quality, well-fitted undershirt can be worn on its own during hot summer days or as part of a casual loungewear outfit. In fact, undershirts with breathability and moisture-wicking properties are perfect as standalone shirts as well. These undershirts often have a slightly thicker fabric, additional detailing (like a pocket), or a more fashionable cut to ensure a polished look that doesn't make you look like you're just wearing a tried-and-true undershirt.

Wearing an undershirt is a wise choice for men seeking both style and practicality. The best undershirts for men will help absorb sweat and prevent it from seeping into your outer garments as sweat marks, keeping you fresh and dry throughout the day. Hence, for men who are prone to sweat, undershirts will really extend the lifespan of your outer garments by acting as an additional layer of protection between them and your body. For men who run hot, undershirts made from breathable materials will also keep you cool by wicking away moisture. The best undershirts will also help enhance comfort by acting as a barrier between your skin and the rough texture of certain fabrics (like itchy wool), reducing irritation and preventing your outer shirt from clinging to your body. During colder seasons, an undershirt also adds an extra layer of warmth.

Sources indicate that the number of undershirts a man should own depends on his personal preference and lifestyle. However, as a general rule of thumb, it's recommended to have a rotation of at least 5 to 7 undershirts to ensure that you have a fresh one for each day of the week. This gives each undershirt ample time to rest and recover between wears and allows for regular washing, ensuring that you always have a fresh undershirt ready. This rotation not only helps prolong their lifespan but also makes sure each undershirt is not subjected to excessive wear and tear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 upcoming EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of newly introduced public EV charging stations.

“The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

Industry observers note that the rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, new data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

In a recent development, I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

If Washington doesn’t see that for, “Go pound sand, eh?” that it is, then it’s truly lost the plot – but even if the “blue wave” last week was enough to shake a little sense into the folks running the show, it may already be too late to patch things up.

The 10 Best Cross-Training Shoes for Women, Tested by Editors

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that OUR FITNESS EDITORS love to slip on cushy sneakers like the Hoka Clifton 11 for our 5Ks and hot girl walks. But on days when we're lifting heavy, doing a functional strength training workout, or have a gym sesh that switches between lifts and sprints, we turn to our favorite cross-training shoes. If you’re unfamiliar with the term, cross-training is combining different exercise modalities—like cardio, resistance training, and plyometric (rapid movements)—during a gym session. Think of these sneakers as multipurpose powerhouses. They keep your feet locked in, whether you’re deadlifting or speed walking on an under-desk treadmill.

Industry observers note that “They’re designed to handle side-to-side movement, quick pivots, and changes in direction—not just forward motion,” claims Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois. “This makes them more supportive for gym workouts, classes, or sports where your foot needs stability in multiple planes, like pickleball or tennis.” On the flip side, a walking or running shoe usually only supports you in straight-line motion, Lockwood says.

Wearing running sneakers for strength training workouts is generally a no-no (except for the caveat about the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 below). All the podiatrists I spoke with say it’s safer and beneficial to invest in cross-training shoes. That’s because they usually have flatter outsoles and thinner midsoles than running shoes to keep your feet locked in, claims Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California. That way, you won’t wobble during your deadlifts and box jumps. The material of cross-training shoes is also more durable than running shoes to resist wear and tear, and has thick heel counters to help prevent ankle injuries.

Whether you're a seasoned weightlifting junkie or a runner on a mission to integrate more training modalities into your routine, read on for the best cross-training shoes you can find.

After testing dozens of cross-training shoes this past year, the latest lululemon Chargefeel 3 stands out for its impeccable support and stability during speedy, lateral movements like ice skaters, kettlebell squats, and Zumba workouts. We’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Despite the fact that sneaker fit and feel is extremely subjective, everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” claims WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

According to recent reports, it’s now 8 ounces instead of 9.1 ounces, and has a lower heel-to-toe drop—6 mm compared to 9.5 mm—to help alleviate stress on the ankles and feet. WH associate style and commerce editor Shannen Zitz loves the wider build for lifting and squatting. She says her feet feel locked in and extra secure. “My feet stay securely in place thanks to a forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter,” says Zitz. She also notes that the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

In a recent development, and post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. “I recently wore these while traveling, and they kept my feet super happy power walking through the airport and standing on long security and customs lines,” Zitz adds. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

Industry observers note that the fit is true to size, and the breathable knit upper doesn’t feel constricting when wearing thick socks (perfect for combating blisters!). Although wide size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, Zitz notes the wide outsole may feel too bulky during quick and dynamic HIIT workouts.

Read More: Every Lululemon Shoe, Ranked.

In a recent development, we wouldn’t recommend most running shoes for cross-training, but the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is an exception. You can effortlessly transition from long runs to deadlifts, thanks to its balanced cushioning and moderate heel-to-toe drop.

Compared to the GTS 24, the latest version has slightly softer cushioning, with about 3 mm more foam in the forefoot and 1 mm in the heel, giving it a smoother, more comfortable feel underfoot. It also drops from 12 mm to 10 mm, creating a slightly more level feel. That can make it feel more stable during strength work than higher-drop running shoes.

Industry observers note that at 9 ounces, it’s a lightweight gem, especially for those with overpronation or flat feet during agility drills. Its GuideRails technology—firm foam on both sides of the foot—keeps feet aligned during everything from Bulgarian split squats to lunges to speed walking. Plus, stiff heel padding keeps feet from sliding."These feel super comfortable and supportive for everyday life, traditional workouts, walks, easy runs—you name it," says Melissa Kendter, CPT, a functional strength coach. "I love that this shoe feels well cushioned but doesn't have a huge chunky sole, making it more appropriate for strength workouts than most running shoes.".

Because the outsole is relatively smooth (it’s built for road miles, not side-to-side gym moves), we’d stick to non-slip floors for quick lateral work. If your workouts are heavy on lifting or plyometrics, a flatter cross-trainer like the Nike Metcon 10 may feel steadier and more secure underfoot.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

We’ve been fans of the Nano series since 2018, and every year we notice Reebok levels up its cushioning and heel stability to keep our feet locked in and comfortable during even the most intense workouts. The midsole padding is firm for balancing during heavy lifts and lateral movements, yet is still bouncy for excellent rebound during HIIT workouts and explosive jumps. The mesh material upper is also firm, keeping you steady when lifting heavy.

According to recent reports, MH digital designer Taryn Colbert used to prefer flat lifestyle shoes like Converse or Vans, but has since switched over to the Nano X5 for her cross-training sessions. The stiffer soles offer her better balance, while she notes that the heel counter is dense, meaning it doesn’t flex easily. However, the 7 mm heel-to-toe drop may be too steep for some weightlifters who prefer a ground-feel shoe. But it’s a pro if you like extra heel support.

Industry observers note that the grippy outsole delivers superior traction when executing deadlifts or weighted squats, while the snug laces never budge. Colbert also notes that the breathable material helps combat sweaty feet. Just note that the fit runs tight (consider ordering at least a half-size up), and it weighs 12.1 ounces, making it one of the heaviest shoes in this guide.

If your workouts focus on dynamic moves like kettlebell swings or heavy lifting, the Nobull Drive is a gem. It’s crafted with a breathable mesh knit upper that feels sock-like and keeps feet cool during grueling reps.

Industry observers note that the balance of flexibility and firmness makes it simple to transition from the squat rack to the HIIT studio. WH associate editor Olivia Luppino wears them during physical therapy to help maintain balance when doing Bosu ball squats, and then hits the gym to do deadlifts. She also notes the mesh isn’t scratchy—an glitch she has had when wearing this material.

The subtle foam feels similar to a minimally-cushioned running shoe, while the low 4 mm drop keeps Luppino grounded when deadlifting. She also notes that a firm heel counter makes her feet feel secure without too much stiffness. And at 8.3 ounces, it’s the lightest shoe in this guide, which makes it an optimal choice for sprints and mixed-modality workouts.

According to recent reports, nike’s latest Metcon 10 is a top pick among our editors when it comes to pumping iron. Its main revision compared to the last iteration is a smaller, stiffer plate strategically placed under the heel to help stabilize the feet when squatting heavy reps or doing deadlifts. It’s also lighter at 11.8 ounces (it was previously 13.3 ounces) and feels more responsive during jumps and HIIT when it’s not leg day.

Zitz was completely sold after her first wear. “I feel totally grounded with the 4 mm drop while squatting and lunging, and they never weigh me down while running,” claims Zitz. “I also love how sleek and stylish they look (especially in the pink color!), and I've been wearing them with nearly every athleisure fit since I got them.”.

Recent findings suggest that the tough rubber traction is another highlight. It feels almost sticky, helping you stay put. Zitz adds that the grooves on the outsole are great for slick sidewalks or dynamic movements, like box jumps. The mesh upper also offers some breathability, but it’s not the most airy shoe in this guide.

Read More: Best Weightlifting Shoes.

The RAD One V2 is so flexible that it feels like an extension of your feet during lifts, drills, and cardio. The forefoot bends easily and delivers bounce that feels natural. Accardi notes her movement feels “controlled, yet free” when these are on her feet. “While firmness is crucial in a cross-training shoe, many are too stiff, which limits power in workouts unrelated to lifting,” she says. “These feel nimble yet stable for agility drills and plyometric moves like box jumps.”.

The moderate 6 mm drop and heel counter provide balance and sturdiness. The springy EVA midsole also alleviates joint impact during high-impact moves. And bonus: the cushioning is wrapped with rubber to help combat wear and tear, while the textured outsole provides perfect traction during lateral bounds and tuck jumps. “My footing feels nice and steady during transitions, whether I’m going fast or slow.”.

In a recent development, note that this kick is the heaviest option in this guide, weighing 12.8 ounces. It’s not the best option for long-distance runs, but it’s a top pick if you’re all about explosive movements.

Recent findings suggest that on is a cult-fave among runners for its cloud-like outsole that’s become a style statement, but the Cloudpulse Pro proves the brand is also a game changer in cross-training shoes. Besides short sprints, it’s designed for workouts that blend cardio and strength—box jumps, sprints, step-ups, and ice skaters. Its signature CloudTec cushioning—compressive foam that absorbs impact—is ultra-bouncy and makes you feel like you’re flying during jumps and agility drills. It propels you forward whether you’re walking, running, or doing dynamic movements. One word that describes it perfectly is energetic. The foam also isn’t overly soft, which is great for support during fast transitions.

Sources indicate that the 6 mm heel-to-toe drop keeps Accardi grounded and balanced during lateral and dynamic movements. A firm heel counter keeps her feet secure, which gives her the confidence to grind hard. Weighing 10.6 ounces, it feels resilient yet solid. The thick, grippy outsole also helps her maintain control on smooth, slick floors. Plus, the polyester material evaporates sweat to keep feet dry.

In a recent development, the fit is roomy, especially in the toe box, making it an excellent option for those with wide feet or bunions. “The fit is perfection,” states WH food producer Tina Martinez. “It’s streamlined through the narrowest part of my foot and hugs my arches in the most secure way.”.

Read More: Best On Shoes for Walking.

In a recent development, if you want a marshmallow-like feel in your cross-training kicks, the While On Earth Move Trainer is a star pick that’s plush minus the bulk. The spongy EVA foam is ideal for short or long runs, while a heel counter (hard plastic that wraps around the heel) prevents any budging during weight training. It’s also light and nimble at 10.6 ounces, making it a workhorse for cardio and strength work.

WH deputy visual editor Dangi McCoy says it’s super supportive during at-home workouts and lateral movements like lunges and shuffling. Plus, it requires no break-in period before hitting the gym. “The width of the shoe itself is great for stability—my feet and toes are secure with any movement,” says McCoy. The wide base and toe box offer ample space for natural foot movement, especially during fast circuit training and intervals, while the neutral 6 mm drop promotes even landings.

Another nice feature: It’s stain and water-resistant. While this shoe is comfortable enough for running, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 24 is better for long runs. But sprints and short-distance running workouts? For sure.

Recent findings suggest that weekly cross-training puts wear and tear on your shoes, so picking a durable pair is a priority. The GORUCK Ballistic Trainer is strong and resilient enough to handle demanding training from plyometrics to climbing. The Cordura nylon upper is abrasion-resistant and strong, while the rubber outsole is thick and sturdy to sustain repetitive force. Accardi has even worn it to rock climb. “The fabric still looks like it did straight out of the box after scraping against a climbing wall,” claims Accardi. “The sole also kept me from slipping on challenging areas.”.

It has been revealed that the 8 mm drop feels level, making it practical for barbell squats or deadlifts, while the EVA foam midsole is plush enough to absorb impact during sprints and jumps. And don’t worry—it doesn’t skimp on stability. A heel counter secures the feet to the insole during weight-bearing exercises. As for fit, a wide toe box allows for comfy movement.

Nike took the best traits of its iconic Free running shoe to create the Metcon 6—a trusty hybrid running and cross trainer. Whether you’re executing agility drills, speed work, or lunges, it delivers the perfect combination of comfort and stability, no matter what workout you have on deck. "This is perfect for my training workouts that consist of part speed run intervals and part strength training because of its combination of cushioning and stability," claims Ashley Barnett, NASM-CPT. She adds that it’s great for jumping, strength routines, and mixed workouts. Accardi also loves wearing it during HIIT classes, highlighting its flexibility and responsiveness when transitioning from burpees to high knees.

In a recent development, compared to the Metcon 10, it has a higher drop at 7.2 mm. While this is a pro in a running shoe, it may mean having less stability during heavy lifts. It’s also worth noting that it fits snug and narrow, so you may have to go up a half size. Accardi has bunions and had to size up to prevent the fabric from rubbing against the sides of her feet during runs and agility drills.

Sources indicate that everyone has a unique foot shape, and each brand can fit differently. So, finding the right fit can be complex. But as a general rule of thumb, your feet should feel supported, not suffocated, and you shouldn't be counting down the minutes until you can kick them off, says Mali Pelham, CPT, C.F.S.C., a personal trainer at Wattage in Chicago.

An easy way to measure if you have enough space is by being able to slide your finger back and forth at the back of the heel. Also, your shoes shouldn’t feel like they’re pinching the middle of your foot—this can lead to tingling and numbness if they’re too tight. If you’re completely unsure, it doesn’t hurt to get fitted at a shoe store. Referencing brands’ sizing charts can also be helpful. Also, pay attention to width, as different brands offer narrow and wide options.

Heel-to-toe drop refers to the height difference between the heel and the forefoot of the shoe.

Consider the type of workouts you'll be tackling in your newly introduced kicks. Each demands specific qualities in a shoe, though the best cross-training shoes for women are versatile enough to let you do all these workouts in them.

In a recent development, the Women’s Health team has spent almost seven years (since 2018!) testing and curating the ultimate guide to the best cross-training shoes for women by putting more than 50 cross-training shoes through their paces. Our rigorous testing process involved multiple phases, including scouring reviews, consulting industry experts, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We laced up cross-trainers for a battery of tests designed to assess performance across various activities, including weightlifting, cardio, agility drills, and CrossFit workouts. Then, we evaluated whether or not a shoe is functional for different kinds of workouts, has enough stability to prevent ankle rolling, is durable enough to withstand wear and tear, and is comfortable for long hours at the gym. #98701. Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1255 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • In a recent development, the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • Sources indicate that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared demonstrates a latest-generation Model Y in traffic.

In a recent development, the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

Sources indicate that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

In a recent development, careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

This isn’t fresh in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Sources indicate that now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

According to recent reports, waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

According to recent reports, tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

In a recent development, since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

In other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

Sources indicate that the penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

It has been revealed that and Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk remarked in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

The Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

We’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

Recent findings suggest that people have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

In a recent development, but police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

It has been revealed that the fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

It has been revealed that NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#98699. How a Former New York City Caviar Factory Became an Art-Filled Oasis of Calm

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

How a Former New York City Caviar Factory Became an Art-Filled Oasis of Calm

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s late Friday afternoon in Manhattan and Alexis Piqueras has misplaced his phone.
  • A break from our harried digital world was what he was seeking when, not long ago, he set out to buy an apartment downtown, having returned to Newly introduced York after a three-year stint in Los Angeles.
  • Piqueras relaxes in the living area of his Manhattan loft with his dogs, Prince and Bridget; artworks by Wolfgang Tillmans (top) and Giangiacomo Rossetti.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s late Friday afternoon in Manhattan and Alexis Piqueras has misplaced his phone. Not that he’s concerned. Bathed in the light of October’s early setting sun, the Spanish-born producer and founder of AP Studio, settles into a Charlotte Perriand dining chair at his Tribeca apartment. The vibe is calm: a mix of warm hues, rich textures, and timeworn woods. Candles perfume the air. And all around us the faces and limbs of figurative artworks seem to join our conversation. “I’ll find it eventually,” Piqueras notes, unperturbed by his absent device.

A break from our harried digital world was what he was seeking when, not long ago, he set out to buy an apartment downtown, having returned to Newly introduced York after a three-year stint in Los Angeles. “Sometimes I need to hide amid the chaos,” states Piqueras, who has built a busy career collaborating with brands on the order of Louis Vuitton, Celine, and Loewe. His real-estate ambitions transcended any simple notions of an urban oasis. Yes, he wanted peace and quiet. But he also wanted some untouched architectural grit that felt true to the city, in particular his visions of its post-industrial 1970s waterfront.

Piqueras relaxes in the living area of his Manhattan loft with his dogs, Prince and Bridget; artworks by Wolfgang Tillmans (top) and Giangiacomo Rossetti.

A Harold Ancart painting and Prince preside over the entry.

Charlotte Perriand chairs and a custom sofa face off across an Alvar Aalto prototype cocktail table; floor lamp by Isamu Noguchi and seascape by Paul Thek.

In a recent development, he found that in Tribeca. Its warehouses and sleepy streets also reminded him of his time in Berlin, where he fell in love with club culture. His latest loft, located in what had once been a 19th-century caviar factory, retains its original brick walls, timber columns, and wood windows, through which he can view slices of the Hudson River. A previous renovation had made smart use of the 2,500 square feet, carving out a primary suite, guest bedroom, office, powder room and pantry alongside the open cooking/living/dining space. It all just needed to be pared back. “The moment you take away everything, you have all you need,” Piqueras indicates.

It has been revealed that working with the Brazilian-born furniture and interior designer Pali Xisto Cornelsen, he stripped back what time-stamped interventions had been made over the years. In the kitchen, they updated the existing high-gloss kitchen cabinetry with white-painted fronts and chunky solid-cherry pulls, also installing stainless-steel countertops and a fresh island, trimmed in wood. The walls were coated in Benjamin Moore’s Simply White, the floorboards refinished, and the windows dressed in linen roman shades. “I was conscious of creating a neutral canvas,” claims Xisto Cornelsen, who removed all the recessed lighting. “You’re gonna feel a certain calm.”.

A David Wojnarowicz artwork hangs above a circa-1960 Knoll console.

The den features a built-in daybed; etchings by David Hockney and photograph by Nan Goldin.

Art introduces faces to that expanse. Working with advisor Joe Sheftel to expand his collection, Piqueras has assembled a sophisticated trove with a focus on works by Queer talents of recent or current memory. Those include photographs by Wolfgang Tillmans, Peter Hujar, and Alvin Baltrop, who documented the pre-AIDS gay revelry of the nearby Hudson River piers. Elsewhere are portraits by Larry Stanton and David Hockney. Some bare bodies, Piqueras admits, have left houseguests blushing. But the intention was never skin for the sake of shock. “It’s a lot about community,” says Sheftel. “The apartment also functions that way, as a fun space for friends and play.” A romantic spirit comes across in still lives (a burning candle by Phoebe Helander) and landscapes ( a Doron Langberg painting of Fire Island Pines). Evident too is Piqueras’s deep love of Fresh York City. “There’s also a narrative of activism—of power and creativity through crisis,” says Sheftel, pointing out works by David Wojnarowicz.

In the dining area, Charlotte Perriand chairs surround a Pierre Chapo table beneath a Paavo Tynell lamp; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans, still life by Phoebe Helander, and portrait by Larry Stanton.

Displayed above the custom DJ station (aka Piqueras’s little Berlin) are works by Wolfgang Tilmans, Seth Baker, and Issy Wood.

A Doron Langberg painting hangs amidst the kitchen’s reimagined cabinetry; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans and stools by Alvar Aalto.

The library features a mix of vintage Scandinavian finds, including a Märta Blomstedt lounge chair, Paavo Tynell pendant light, and a desk and side chair by Axel Einar Hjorth. The large-scale photograph is by Wolfgang Tillmans and the shelves display works by Alvin Baltrop, David Wojnarowicz, Jacob Littlejohn, Peter Hujar, and Giangiacomo Rossetti. Resting on the floor is an etching by David Hockney.

A Hunter Reynolds artwork takes pride of place above Piqueras’s bed; speakers by Ojas.

The primary bath retains the building’s original brickwork.

According to recent reports, elsewhere throughout the interiors, they added custom millwork, including the office’s daybed and wall-mounted desk, the living area’s bookshelves, and the dining area’s DJ station, a corner Piqueras calls his little Berlin. Tapered silhouettes and bevels soften edges. “There are all these happy surprises,” indicates Cornelsen, who referenced design heroes like Le Corbusier, Joaquim Tenreiro, and Jean Prouvé. Vintage furniture adds to that neutral rhapsody, with choice finds by Pierre Chapo, Isamu Noguchi, and Alvar Aalto, whose coffee table prototype anchors the living area. It is joined by a cast of other Scandinavian characters, among them light fixtures by Paavo Tynell, the upholstered Märta Blomstedt lounge chair where Piqueras enjoys his morning tea, and pieces by Axel Einar Hjorth.

According to recent reports, collecting and decorating, Piqueras has found, are not unlike his daily profession. “Renovating an apartment is a kind of production,” he says. “My skill is to orchestrate.” But it’s a break from the grind that he now gets to relish at home. “Work is insane. The streets are insane. But then I can come here,” he says. “I put down my phone—and then I don’t think about it.”.

A Paavo Tynell pendant crowns the guest bedroom, which features more custom millwork and displays artworks by Precious Okoyomon (left) and Christopher Culver.

A Wolfgang Tillmans photograph takes the place of the guest bath’s vanity mirror.

A Sol LeWitt artwork rests on the den’s custom desk; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans and chair by Axel Einar Hjorth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that volkswagen is turning one of its best-selling nameplates into an electric SUV.
  • In a recent development, the ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the newly introduced ID.
  • Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that volkswagen is turning one of its best-selling nameplates into an electric SUV. The new ID. Tiguan is now rolling off the assembly line and will replace the ID.4 in 2027.

In a recent development, the ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the newly introduced ID. Tiguan will replace them in Volkswagen’s EV lineup next year.

Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID. Tiguan is the next model to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the manufacturer calls it.

The latest electric SUV adopts Volkswagen’s best-selling nameplate, the Tiguan, as part of its shift away from the numerical system used on the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5.

Recent findings suggest that volkswagen confirmed on Thursday that series production of the electric ID. Tiguan has now begun at its Embden Plant in Germany.

“The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer stated last month after unveiling the new SUV. He added that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”.

It has been revealed that the ID. Tiguan will be a step change from its predecessors, the ID.4 and ID.5, featuring Volkswagen’s “Pure Positive” design language, which includes an overhauled interior and exterior design and updated tech.

Volkswagen stated the ID. Tiguan’s “hallmark feature” is the completely redesigned exterior. The fresh design remains closer to the gas-powered Tiguan, with a boxy, traditional SUV look.

According to recent reports, unlike the ID.4’s aerodynamic design, the upcoming ID. Tiguan features a wide, chunky front end and traditional pull-style door handles instead of the flush ones.

It has been revealed that in Volkswagen’s words, the new ID. Tiguan electric SUV “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment.”.

Sources indicate that inside, the updates are just as evident. The overhauled interior features Volkswagen’s new infotainment setup, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and a 15″ center display. There’s also an optional 12″ passenger screen available.

Another highlight is the return of physical buttons. After listening to customer feedback from current drivers, Volkswagen added physical buttons under the center display and on the steering wheel for climate control and other vehicle functions.

To spark a bit of nostalgia, VW added a fun latest Retro Mode feature that transforms the Digital Cockpit and center display to mimic the style of iconic models like the first-generation Golf.

Drivers can also choose from six classic VW models to display in a virtual “garage” on the infotainment screen: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg, and Beetle.

The new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:.

Recent findings suggest that depending on the configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a “upcoming benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe with a WLTP range of up to 377 miles (607 km).

In a recent development, volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Tiguan in Germany and a few other European markets in October, starting at €42,695 ($47,800). It’s available in three trims: Trend, Life, and Style.

Sources indicate that after it launches in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in North America to replace the ID.4.

In a recent development, apparently, the upcoming ID Tiguan has a slightly better Cx (Drag Coefficient) at 0.26 versus 0.28 on first gen ID4 and 0.27 on 2nd gen. According to VW, it’s achieved using front air curtains, a minimal air intake, an enclosed underbody, and a longer roof spoiler.

In a recent development, volkswagen said prices and other details will come in “due course.” The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.

Industry observers note that since the European model offers close to 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.

Official US prices have not yet been confirmed. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of about $45,000, so the ID. Tiguan will likely be priced similarly.

The NBA season is in full swing—and so is the holiday season. NBA swag always makes for a solid, low-effort gift for fans of the Association, and we’re always on top of the latest collabs. The National Basketball Association’s latest venture, though, might be its most accessible to date, and it’s one we didn’t really see coming: Amazon Essentials x NBA.

Shop the Amazon Essentials x NBA Collection.

Amazon Essentials x NBA Men's Family Pajama Sets, Knicks.

BYD launched the Denza N8 EV in China, a five-seat luxury SUV that promises more than 1,000 km (621 miles) of CLTC range, a tech-filled cabin, and plenty of premium extras.

In a recent development, another day, another new BYD vehicle is now on sale in China. After opening preorders for the Denza N8 EV a few weeks ago, BYD held the grand launch event on Thursday.

The new N8 EV, or “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza called it, is available in six variants, including four battery-electric (EV) and two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain options.

In a recent development, the all-electric Denza N8 starts at 269,900 yuan, or about $40,500, with prices ranging up to 329,900 yuan ($49,500) for the Flagship model. The PHEV models start at 300,900 yuan and 32,900 yuan, respectively.

Measuring 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, the Denza N8 EV is slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

Inside, the interior is pretty over the top with a huge 30″ panoramic infotainment screen that stretches nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard. There’s also a newly introduced 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

BYD added a few premium extras like front and rear zero-gravity seats, a drop-down ceiling entertainment screen, ambient lighting, and wireless phone chargers.

Recent findings suggest that the Denza N8 is offered with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD variant uses a single motor that delivers either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp), depending on the configuration.

In a recent development, the tri-motor Denza N8 debuts BYD’s e3 Evo technology. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

BYD’s Denza said the N8 EV boasts an all-electric CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles), “making it the world’s longest-range mass-produced all-electric SUV.”.

To put it in perspective, that’s as much as the outgoing N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

It’s available with two second-gen BYD Blade battery packs: 105.792 kWh and 130.15 kWh, delivering CLTC ranges of up to 885 km (549 miles) and 1,003 km (623 miles).

Sources indicate that with BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, the Denza N8 EV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. Charging from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Like many of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is equipped with BYD’s premium tech and features, such as its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system and God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system.

BYD also sells the extended Denza N8L in China, which went on sale earlier this year, starting at 299,800 yuan ($45,000).
